summary: Fort Niagara Light at the mouth of the Niagara River: lit 1823 on the fort's mess-house, a 1872 stone tower, dark since 1993, in Fort Niagara State Park.

lens.where: visitor center, Old Fort Niagara (LighthouseFriends; Discover Upstate)

structures.note: Octagonal stone tower with brick lining (USLHS). About 50 feet (15 m) when built, raised 11 ft 4 in with a brick watch room in 1900 (LighthouseFriends; SeaTheLights); USLHS gives 60 ft base to lantern centre.
Square iron oil house, 540-gallon capacity, 25 feet south of the tower (LighthouseFriends; USLHS gives c. 1900-1905).
Two-story, six-room keeper's dwelling 140 feet west of the tower, Queen Anne (USLHS gives 1897 and wood). Contract dated 25 June 1896 (Board reports; LighthouseFriends).
Squat wooden tower on the mess-house inside the fort, replaced by the 1872 tower (LighthouseFriends; SeaTheLights).

staffing.note: Last keeper in these sources: Edward Wallingford Moon (1934 to at least 1939). No keeper is named after the 1939 record.

access.note: Inside Fort Niagara State Park, near the French Castle. Hours differ by source: LighthouseFriends says weekends mid-July through August; Discover Upstate lists free self-guided tours noon to 3 p.m. from mid-July to mid-October. Check before going.

facts.agency: Old Fort Niagara Association (manages the light); ownership given as U.S. Coast Guard (LighthouseFriends) and New York State (Discover Upstate)

events.note: British beacon on the roof of the French Castle inside the fort; a predecessor light, in use until 1803 (LighthouseFriends; SeaTheLights)
Roof light remains active until 1803 (LighthouseFriends)
Congress provides $1,000 on 7 May 1822 for a lamp on the mess-house (LighthouseFriends)
Station established: lamp in a squat wooden tower on the mess-house; USLHS gives 1823; Putnam lists Fort Niagara among the 1823 lights
William Morgan held at the fort shortly before his disappearance; LighthouseFriends says keeper Edward Giddings was suspected and never arrested (roster lists Ezekiel Jewett as keeper)
Naval Lieutenant Charles T. Platt reports the light at 70 feet above the water, with nine lamps and reflectors, and credits the keeper (quoted by LighthouseFriends; the primary report was not read)
Tornado damages the keeper's dwelling and outbuildings (LighthouseFriends only)
Fourth-order Fresnel lens and new lantern in the stone tower (LighthouseFriends; Discover Upstate). USLHS gives 1859 as the original lens year
Lighthouse Board asks for a new light; the wooden tower let in snow and rain; a chimney spark caused a roof fire (LighthouseFriends)
Congress provides $16,000 for a new lighthouse on 3 March 1871; work begins July 1871 and stops 30 November (LighthouseFriends)
Octagonal limestone tower completed (fifty feet originally; USLHS 1872); fourth-order lens moved from the old tower
Light first exhibited 10 June 1872 (LighthouseFriends)
Board requests $4,000 for a new keeper's dwelling; LighthouseFriends quotes the Board calling the old house unsuitable
Steel water tank on the military reservation, which obscured the light from lake points, is moved (Board report)
Keeper's dwelling rebuilt under a contract of 25 June 1896 (Board reports); six-room, two-story house 140 feet west of the tower (LighthouseFriends)
Iron handrail in the tower stairway; 289 running feet of sidewalk; various repairs (Board report)
Board requests $2,000 for a small light at the mouth of the river, a request repeated for six years (Board appropriation list; LighthouseFriends)
Stone tower built up with brick 11 feet 4 inches; watch room added below the lantern; focal plane raised by the same amount (Board report; LighthouseFriends)
Square iron oil house, 540-gallon capacity, erected 25 feet south of the tower (LighthouseFriends 1905; SeaTheLights 1900; USLHS c. 1900-1905)
3 February 1917: Keeper George F. Ferguson helps three fishermen on the ice near the light station (Bulletin). LighthouseFriends gives a young man whose boat was caught in an ice jam
Light electrified on 28 August 1919; characteristic changed to four seconds of light and a two-second eclipse (LighthouseFriends); Commissioner list shows the light as electric incandescent
Seized speedboat carrying 400 gallons of alcohol to the Coast Guard station catches fire; Keeper Ferguson and a deputy sheriff escape (LighthouseFriends only)
Edward Wallingford Moon appointed keeper (USLHS: 1934 to at least 1939)
Tower opened to visitors during the week marking the 150th anniversary of the Lighthouse Service (LighthouseFriends, citing the Niagara Falls Gazette)
NRIS record gives 19 July 1984 as its date published; the record's PDF is 22 KB
Coast Guard decommissions the light rather than trim trees, and replaces it with a light on a nearby radio tower (LighthouseFriends; USLHS year discontinued 1993)
Fresnel lens removed from the tower and placed on display at the visitor center at Old Fort Niagara (LighthouseFriends)
Windows replaced with a $10,000 donation from the East Hill Foundation (LighthouseFriends)

corrections.why: USLHS gives 89.5 feet above water (about 27.3 m). LighthouseFriends says the focal plane was raised 11 ft 4 in in 1900; 24.4 m (80 ft) matches neither source.

LighthouseFriends says the 1919 electrification allowed a change to four seconds of light and a two-second eclipse, from fixed white. That is the derived Light List form for the last characteristic. No source here gives a green light for the Fort Niagara tower. The proposed form is derived, not quoted.

resolved_conflicts.explanation: The record's 1781 date (Rowlett) is the British roof light inside the French Castle, a predecessor that was in use until 1803 (LighthouseFriends). The present station is dated 1823 (USLHS; Putnam; LighthouseFriends).
The tower was about 50 feet when built and was raised 11 ft 4 in in 1900, which accounts for USLHS's 60 feet to lantern centre.
LighthouseFriends dates the 540-gallon iron oil house to 1905; SeaTheLights gives 1900; the USLHS record gives 'ca. 1900-1905'. The story gives all three.

The NPGallery record (NRIS 84002809) gives 'Date Published' 7/19/1984, which is a publication date rather than a stated listing date. Its PDF is 22 KB, the same size as the Buffalo Main and Cedar Island records, so it appears to be a placeholder.

notes_for_editor: The NRHP nomination is not digitised on NPGallery (its NPGallery record gives a file size of 22151 bytes, the same size as the Buffalo Main and Cedar Island records, so it appears to be a placeholder), so the nomination was not read. Wikipedia was not read. Platt's 1838 report and the 1826 Morgan affair are known only through LighthouseFriends; the primary documents were not located in the corpus (no volume before 1891 for the Board). The 1871 appropriation and the 1868 request are also LighthouseFriends-only. Conflicts that the story states: 1917 rescue (Bulletin: three fishermen on the ice; LighthouseFriends: a young man in an ice jam); original lens year (LighthouseFriends and Discover Upstate 1857; USLHS 1859); keeper Mason's last year (USLHS 1914, LighthouseFriends 1913); ownership (LighthouseFriends: Coast Guard; Discover Upstate: New York State); automation and lens removal (Discover Upstate: automated 1983, lens in the tower until 1983; LighthouseFriends: decommissioned 1993, lens removed 1995). The keeper named Edward Giddings in LighthouseFriends' Morgan account is not on the USLHS roster for 1826, and the story does not link him to the 1826 keeper's post. The 1929 Cleveland Clinic fire and Ferguson's presence are from LighthouseFriends alone; the story does not relay his medical history. The 1926 speedboat fire is from LighthouseFriends alone. Current hours are from two listings that disagree; the Old Fort Niagara site has no lighthouse page reachable from here, so check before publishing. The Board volume for 1896-97 (archive.org annualreportlig02statgoog) has no page index in the corpus, so entries 1200 and 1206 are cited to the volume without a scan page. The Commissioner's electric incandescent list entry (scan page 529) is read from the corpus OCR, so the quote uses only the clean words. Discover Upstate's 'mid-July 13 through mid- October' phrasing is unclear; the story gives only mid-July to mid-October. Fact-check 2026-10-22: the 1917 Bulletin notice (cite 11) is OCR'd from a two-column page. The OCR reads the Fort Niagara entry (3 February 1917, Keeper George F. Ferguson) and a rescue of three fishermen on the ice in the vicinity of the light, but it also places a Port Austin Reef (Mich.) assistant keeper in the same notice, so whether Ferguson alone or with that assistant made the rescue is not settled. The story names Ferguson only as the keeper in the notice and does not say what he did. The page image was not opened: a navigation to the uslhs.org PDF produced a file download prompt, which was not accepted, and it was not retried. Check the page image before publishing. The 1896-97 Board volume has no page index in the archive, so entries 1200 and 1206 carry no scan page. Fort Niagara's 1900 oil house is dated 1900 by SeaTheLights, 1905 by LighthouseFriends, and c. 1900-1905 by the USLHS; the story says so. The 1929 Cleveland Clinic detail is kept to the sourced fact of the fire; the medical detail LighthouseFriends gives is left out. Board volume scan pages checked with corpus.py page: 1894 dwelling and tank at scan p.500 and dwelling request at p.336; 1899 entry 73 at p.206, appropriation at p.72; 1900 entry 73 at p.183. Putnam (scan p.205) lists Fort Niagara among the 1823 lights.
